did_you_know.text: The verse accuses Ephraim and the house of Israel of deceit and treachery, and it also mentions that Judah stands before the Lord and is judged according to its faithfulness and actions.
Ephraim is described as one who “feeds on the wind” and pursues the “east wind”—an image of futile effort—while also making a treaty with Assyria and sending oil to Egypt.
The Lord presents his case against Judah as a legal dispute and declares that he will punish Jacob according to his ways and deeds.
Hosea recalls Jacob from birth: he grasped his brother’s heel and later wrestled with God—an account that emphasizes his character as one who struggles and strives.
Jacob’s story includes weeping and pleading, as well as a reference to Bethel, where he found God and where God spoke with him.
Through the reference to Jacob, the prophet calls Israel to return to its God, to keep kindness and justice, and to wait for him continually.
Ephraim is described as using dishonest scales and loving to oppress; thus, wealth accumulated through unfair trade is presented as a moral sin.

Ephraim boasts of its wealth and claims that no wrongdoing has been found in it, but the Lord reminds them that he has been their God since the exodus from Egypt and promises to bring his people back to tents, as in the days of the festival.
The Lord says that he spoke to his people through the prophets, gave many visions, and used them to present images—testimony to the various ways prophetic revelation and warning were delivered.

The chapter connects Jacob, who worked in Aram, with Israel, who came out of Egypt and was preserved through a prophet. It concludes by emphasizing that Ephraim will bear responsibility for its anger, bloodshed, and disgrace.
